Today is National Truth & Reconciliation day, a day to meant to recognize the horrific traumas of Canada’s genocide and ongoing disposition of Indigenous peoples. Given the white nationalist gathering at Kamloops Indian Residential School, I felt compelled to share some images I made there a number of years ago.

For over a century, the Canadian state worked with the Catholic Church to forcefully separate children from their families. These children were re-educated, malnourished, tortured, abused, and many died. The sites of these atrocities are still standing. You needn’t just look overseas or to the history books to see Canada’s participation in colonization.

The white nationalists who gathered at Kamloops are not a fluke, they are the result of an ongoing attempt to delegitimization the violent history of Canadian colonialism and Residential Schools. This viewpoint has morphed from a fringe far right opinion into a commonly held idea among “common sense” conservatives. It is not enough to ignore or consider such thinking as fringe, it must be challenged clearly and swiftly for the survivors and the victims.

We cannot be tempted by forgetfulness. These actions were undertaken by men and women, we cannot forget the feeling of hatred this history makes us feel; we cannot forget the sacrifice. To paraphrase Walter Benjamin’s Theses on The Philosophy of History, these wish to correct this history is nourished by the image of enslaved ancestors rather than that of liberated grandchildren.

We find the remnants of this genocidal legacy in the ground, air, and waters surrounding us. It is a history has not yet been reconciled for.

Janosch ist im Alter von 95 Jahren gestorben. 😢

Du hast uns nicht erklärt, wie man glücklich wird. Du hast uns gezeigt, wie wenig man dafür manchmal braucht.

Janosch hat uns gelehrt, dass Freundschaft wichtiger ist als Besitz, dass Fantasie keine Grenzen kennt und dass das Glück oft dort wartet, wo wir längst zu Hause sind.

Seine Geschichten waren nie nur für Kinder. Sie waren auch kleine Lebensweisheiten für Erwachsene.

💛 Danke, Janosch. Für das Lachen, die Wärme und die Erinnerungen.

I genuinely had SUCH A GREAT TIME with this movie!

Bill Hader brings the iconic Cat in the Hat to life in an animated adventure that celebrates everything I’ve always appreciated about Dr. Seuss.

The WHIMSY.

The IMAGINATION.

The ABSURD HUMOR.

The pure JOY of storytelling!

And man, this movie is FUNNY.

The kind of movie where the entire family can laugh out loud together!

But what makes this film so special isn’t just the comedy.

IT’S THE HEART.

Underneath all the ridiculous adventures is a beautiful story about family, understanding our parents, and the sacrifices they continuously make for us.

Sometimes children don’t understand WHY their parents make certain choices.

They only see the things they’re leaving behind.

The memories.

The places.

The comfort of what they’ve always known.

But what this movie does so beautifully is remind us that those decisions often come from LOVE.

And that moving forward doesn’t mean forgetting the past.

It means learning to appreciate the PRESENT while embracing everything the FUTURE still has to offer.

As a parent, that message is something I REALLY appreciated.

It’s imaginative, hilarious, meaningful, and filled with the kind of emotional storytelling that makes great family entertainment so special.

A wonderful surprise that I’d absolutely recommend for families!

Martin McDonagh has always been an incredibly fascinating filmmaker to me.

A storyteller who understands how to find humor in the darkest aspects of humanity while never forgetting the sadness hiding beneath it all.

And his latest film continues that tradition.

Starring JOHN MALKOVICH and SAM ROCKWELL as two CIA agents sent to Easter Island shortly before the 1973 Chilean coup, WILD HORSE NINE initially presents itself as another darkly comedic story filled with McDonagh’s signature dialogue and deeply flawed characters.

But beneath the humor is something far more REFLECTIVE.

A story about REGRET.

About MORTALITY.

About GUILT.

And the realization that you can’t always escape the person you’ve spent your entire life becoming.

There’s something especially compelling about a film that doesn’t need to be constantly loud or dramatic to explore something meaningful.

Sometimes it’s the quiet conversations, the uncomfortable silences, and the moments where characters are forced to confront themselves that leave the biggest impression.

And that’s what I appreciate about WILD HORSE NINE.

A strange, somber, and thought-provoking journey that reminds us how complicated people can be.

Democrats got walloped in 2024 and have since sought to understand why. One theory has been that Kamala Harris didn’t do enough “new media.” She didn’t go on Joe Rogan’s podcast or spend enough time in the online spaces where swing voters, young men and low-information voters increasingly get their news. There is truth to that critique. But that doesn’t mean every platform, personality or form of outreach is politically wise. Take the party’s recent flirtation with Hasan Piker.

Piker, a 34-year-old left-wing Twitch streamer, has millions of followers online. Notable progressives — including Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vermont), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York), Rep. Ilhan Omar (Minnesota) and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani — have recently sought to capitalize on his platform. The argument for engaging him, which New York Times columnist Ezra Klein recently articulated, usually goes like this: Democracy requires tough conversations. Democrats ought to engage with different voices and resist the temptation to cancel anyone. They need to expand their reach and show up in more places.

Piker certainly fits that bill, but the downside of associating with him is significant. The internet personality has described Orthodox Jews as “inbred,” said “America deserved 9/11,” asserted “Hamas a thousand times better” than Israel and called the collapse of the Soviet Union “one of the greatest catastrophes of the 20th century.” In a podcast interview with a former Obama speechwriter last week, he called the Republican Party the “biggest terrorist internationally.” Other Democrats have openly rejected his views. Democratic Rep. Ritchie Torres (New York) called Piker “the poster child for the post-October 7th outbreak of antisemitism in America.”

The congressman is right. Piker’s rhetoric, moreover, reinforces caricatures Republicans have spent years attaching to Democrats: that they are weak, anti-American, extreme and culturally alienating.

Consider how the GOP is already punishing Democratic candidates for fraternizing with Piker.

When Trump announced last week that he would be handing down a pardon of Hernandez, those who believed Trump’s anti-dr*g trafficking tirades were shocked at his sudden change of heart.\xa0

During Hernandez’ trial, it was revealed that the former president had orchestrated an extensive dr*g smuggling operation including giving military-grade weapons like grenade launchers to the cartels. Hernandez also accepted a $1 million bribe from cartels and bragged about shoving dr*gs up “Gringos noses.”

Coverage of the pardon has focused on the hypocrisy of the Trump administration, but the truth of this issue goes much deeper. Earlier this year, longtime Trump advisor Roger Stone published a blog calling on Trump to pardon Hernandez so that he might regain power in Honduras and save an experiment in tech bro paradise known as Prospera.\xa0

Prospera, founded with funding from tech bros Peter Thiel, Sam Altman and others, operates on a small island in Honduras previously solely populated with an Afro-indigenous population. The city-state operates almost entirely independent of the country, including its own justice system in the form of 3 retired Arizona judges who rule via zoom.\xa0

When Prospera was created, they relied on then-president Hernandez to create special zones and set up a loose oversight organization which he loaded with his allies. Now that he is out of office, the liberal government has begun asking questions about Prospera, complaining about their lack of investment in the region, and have attempted to back out of agreements that require them to pay significant fines if the community fails.\xa0

As the Honduran government turned against Prospera, the founders spent half a million dollars in the US to buy support from elected officials, urging them to sanction Honduras and deny visas to its politicians. Now, it appears they are banking on the election of a Trump-backed conservative candidate to ensure Prospera can continue its uninterrupted plundering of the region.

Under the Fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act which went into effect late last year, the Selective Service System will now be able to tap into existing government data, such as Social Security Administration information, to automatically register all 18- to 26-year-old men. The deadline to implement the system is in December of this year. 

Previously, men were required to register themselves for the draft when they turned 18. Failure to do so was considered a felony and carried potential financial fines and even prison time. In 40 states, it also limited their ability to receive a driver’s license. 
Opponents of automatic registration believe allowing the Selective Service System to access other government databases is an invasion of privacy.

The system may also automatically register men who are ineligible to serve, like those with certain disabilities. It would then be on those individuals to notify the government that they were registered incorrectly.

Pope Leo XIV just made history by becoming the first sitting Pope to vote in an American election.

Born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, Leo is still registered to vote in suburban Illinois, despite now living in Vatican City. He also holds citizenship in Peru, where he spent more than 20 years as a missionary priest and bishop.

Vatican City doesn’t have political elections (it’s an absolute monarchy), but apparently that hasn’t stopped the Pope from doing his civic duty. On Friday, the Vatican confirmed that Leo had mailed in his ballot for Tuesday’s midterm elections.

And while the Vatican generally avoids getting involved in American elections, Leo hasn’t exactly been shy about criticizing the Trump administration. He’s spoken out against the administration’s treatment of immigrants, questioned whether its policies reflect Christian values, and warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence, particularly its potential to undermine human dignity and replace human workers.

So we don’t know who the Pope voted for, but he’s certainly had a few things to say about the people running the country.

Donald Trump has suffered a massive political defeat. Democrats have taken control of both chambers of Congress, the House and the Senate. So what does this mean for Trump?

Midterm elections don't choose the President; they decide who controls Congress. Trump remains President until January 20, 2029, but he will no longer face a Congress controlled by his own party.

Biggest shocks of the night:
• Texas: Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, ending a 37-year Democratic Senate drought.
• Michigan: Abdul El-Sayed won his Senate race, becoming the first Muslim senator in American history.
• Trump claimed Republicans would have won by a landslide if he had been on the ballot.

3 major changes for Trump:
1. Laws and legislation: any major new law, tax cut or legislative proposal now faces much stronger opposition. Trump can veto, but he can't force Congress to approve his plans.
2. Money: Congress controls federal spending, so military budgets, defence spending, support for Israel and Iran-related funding will face much greater scrutiny.
3. Investigations and accountability: after the February 28 strikes on Iran without congressional authorisation, Democrats can now launch investigations, hold hearings, demand documents and scrutinise the administration.

The limit: Trump is still Commander-in-Chief. Any bill restricting military operations or cutting funding could face his veto, and overriding it needs a two-thirds majority in both chambers. Democrats cannot simply end a war overnight.

Set entirely in a rundown church basement, the musical follows 8 strangers attending an internet addiction support group and sharing their struggles through songs about social media, memes, Candy Crush, Twitter discourse, Reddit threads, cancel culture, dating apps, incels, and porn addiction. It’s entirely a cappella, filled with intricate, complex and sometimes discordant harmonies. For the last two years, I’ve been quietly working on creating a company I’ve hoped to come across but couldn’t find. A tour company that doesn’t just adapt to the lesbian & sapphic travel market, but curates itineraries for us from the jump. One that offers a wide portfolio of itineraries around the world - because it’s a common misconception that queer people only want to travel for pride related events. One that hires sapphic tour leaders, prioritizes building itineraries that support local lgbtq+/women-owned businesses, and thinks about safety from an intersectional lens. 

I deeply believe that queer people deserve to see the world just like everyone else, and that it’s safer (and more joyful!) when you don’t have to explain or shrink yourself to fit in while doing it. So, I built it myself.

For Sydney, that story began during a semester studying abroad in Morocco, a trip that completely changed the trajectory of her life. Years later, after deciding to stop waiting and set off on a year of solo travel, her online community started asking if they could come along too.

What started as a few Sapphic LGBTQ+ group trips quickly became something much bigger.

To all the women reading this, we want to hear from you. What does women’s rights mean to you? What needs to change or improve in society? Have you ever experienced discrimination, harassment, or felt unsafe simply because you are a woman? What changes would make you feel safer, more respected, and more independent?

At Haq Productions, we cover international affairs and geopolitics, but how can we be satisfied with our work if the people around us are still struggling for dignity, equality, and safety? Women's rights are not merely a local, national, or household issue. They are a global issue that deserves attention from every society and every media platform, regardless of its speciality.

This is our first international collaboration, and we are genuinely grateful to everyone who took the time to share their perspectives and contribute to these articles. Bringing together voices from different countries, professions, cities, cultures, and backgrounds has been a meaningful experience for us.

[{'caption': 'The finger-pointing has begun at Fox News following Democrats’ sweeping victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections. During Wednesday’s episode of The Five, a discussion about Republicans losing control of the House and Senate turned into a debate over whether Congress or President Donald Trump deserved the blame.

Emily Compagno argued that Republicans had wasted nearly two years of controlling Washington. She called Congress “really unproductive,” criticizing lawmakers for taking extended breaks and failing to pass legislation that voters had been promised. But Dana Perino raised a different point: wasn’t it the president’s responsibility to lead Congress and get lawmakers behind his plans?

Former Democratic Congressman Harold Ford Jr. immediately picked up on that question. “And he didn’t. That’s what you’re saying, right?” he asked. Compagno pushed back, insisting Congress had failed. Ford responded that presidents are supposed to set the agenda, arguing that Trump had focused on passing his “One Big Beautiful Bill” without pushing lawmakers to accomplish much else. “And guess what? That’s why he lost the House and Senate,” Ford said.

Compagno continued defending Trump, blaming Republican lawmakers for failing to turn his executive orders into permanent laws. She also acknowledged that younger voters were frustrated with the party and that Americans had felt the financial effects of tariffs without seeing the promised benefits.

The exchange offered a glimpse into the conversations now taking place among Republicans following their election losses. Compagno maintained that Congress had failed the president, Ford argued that the president had failed to lead Congress, and Perino’s question brought Trump’s own responsibility into the discussion.
